newsitem.title: UK: London gold softer and sluggish in early Europe.
newsitem.headline: London gold softer and sluggish in early Europe.

text.p: Gold prices drifted lower early on Tuesday after being sold down previously in New York and Asian markets.
"It's quiet this morning but the trend is clearly lower," a dealer said.
Gold was fixed at $319.00 an ounce, compared to $321.70 on Monday afternoon and a London close of $320.60/$321.10.
Dealers said gold started coming under pressure from speculative selling late on Monday after proving unable to hurdle resistance at $322.50.
Then Australian producer selling emerged during Asian trading hours, which also helped depress prices, they added.
"The threat of producer and central bank sales is going to continue capping the market. As it drifts lower it may look at the upside again but ultimately the $300 level is likely," a dealer said.
Analysts noted that gold's first downside target would be the $315 area and then the 12-year low of $313.60 hit last week.
News that Australia's central bank had sold 167 tonnes from its gold reserves sent prices spiralling lower as investors pulled out of the market and speculators bet prices would sink still further.
Silver was also lower at $4.25/$4.27, down four cents from Monday's already weaker London close.
A drop below the $4.23 low of last week would leave silver vulnerable to decline to the September 1993 low of $3.88, analysts said.
Platinum and palladium were more stable, fixing little changed from Monday's levels at $403.50 and $172.00 respectively.
Russia's metal export agency Almazjuvelirexport confirmed it had resumed long-delayed deliveries of platinum group metals to Japan and said the first supplies left Russia on July 8.
But Sergei Gorny, a deputy director of the agency, declined to say how much platinum and palladium Russia would export this year.
Dealers said the confirmation came as no surprise and therefore the market failed to react.
"That's last week's news," a dealer said. "The market's easier and will continue to ease," he added.
Parcels of material may come onto the spot market, helping to gradually lower prices in the still-tight market, he said. --Lida Poletz, London newsroom +44 171 542 2936
